brief.head: BS, decoded
brief.text: For years Amit Varma admired Ajay Shah’s modesty about his “BS article”. BS, it turned out, meant *Business Standard*, where Shah has written a column for thirty years. {127-J02}

brief.head: A dialect with an army
brief.text: There is no reason for Hindi to be inherently superior to Bhojpuri or Maithili, Amit Varma said: a language is a dialect with an army. {127-J14}

brief.head: Malign, and inept too
brief.text: Stretching Hanlon’s razor, Amit Varma said the state should be assumed both malign and incompetent: incompetent because it imagines it can do far more than it can. {127-J16}

brief.head: Markets, civilised
brief.text: Markets are not a feature of capitalism but the invention of civilisation: Ajay Shah thought it was the Soviet leader Gorbachev who said so. {127-J20}

brief.head: Watchers and doers
brief.text: Amit Varma quoted Neil Simon: the world has watchers and doers. He called Ajay Shah a doer, admitting he is sometimes happy being a watcher himself. {127-J23}

thought.text: How we spend our days, of course, is how we spend our lives.
thought.who: Annie Dillard’s line, which Amit Varma quotes so often that people joke about it

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah share what shaped them
lead.head: Ten lenses, two lives
body: “You come here for enlightenment, but today we will give you intimacy,” Amit Varma told listeners. {127-J01}
In the 127th episode of *Everything is Everything*, he and Ajay Shah each offered five frameworks that, looking back, had shaped how they think and who they became.
It was meant to be recorded before a live Life Lessons audience in Goa, but it rained, in October.

Shah explained what binds the ten together. Reasoning from first principles, he said, “really is our greatest defence against all the bullshit of the world”, and it needs a toolkit of basic frameworks. {127-C01}
## How the world works

Varma began with natural selection, which he said should not be left to biology classes. Knowing how evolution wired us, he argued, helps us decide which tendencies to dampen and which to amplify. {127-C02}

Shah’s first was the lesson he would give his 20-year-old self: the world is complex. Randomness, nonlinearity and information scattered everywhere make it far harder to understand and control than we think, he said. {127-C03}

Varma extended that with spontaneous order. Language, common law and above all the economy are shaped from the bottom up, with prices serving as the language through which strangers meet each other’s needs. {127-C04}
## The state and the market

Shah then turned to the state, which Indians, he said, tend to treat as a benevolent mother. He corrected that with Max Weber’s definition of the state as a monopoly of violence, and with public choice theory: the people who run it pursue their own goals. {127-C05}
Varma’s next framework was the double thank-you moment. When buyer and seller thank each other, both are better off, and every voluntary exchange adds to human welfare. {127-C06}

Shah’s defence against the coercive state was rule of law, which at its core means taking discretion away from civil servants: over what is a crime, whom to investigate and whom to prosecute. {127-C07}
Varma added a bonus from Francis Fukuyama. The Indian state does many things badly, he said, when it should do a few things well, beginning with rule of law. {127-C08}
## How to live

The last frameworks turned inward. Varma’s, taken from a chess grandmaster, is “I play to play”: work for the beauty of it, not the outcome. Even Sisyphus can be happy, he argued, if the point of rolling the rock is to roll the rock. {127-C09}
Desires borrowed from others are thin, he said; the ones truly your own are thick. {127-C10}
Shah’s slogan was that life is not a spectator sport. “I’d rather play my own shitty cricket,” he said, than watch the world’s heroes play. {127-C11}
Varma, who quotes Annie Dillard so often that people joke about it, said a life is an accumulation of days, to be lived one at a time. {127-C12}
Shah added that a lifetime, set against a complex world, is too big to plan and breeds apathy. {#hundredyears} “A day, on the other hand, is a tangible problem,” he said.
His last framework was to give unconditionally, without keeping score of favours. Giving, he said, makes us happier and frees the mind. {127-C13}
Varma, who has known Shah for many years, vouched for him. “In this particular case, do as he does, he’s actually done it,” he told listeners. {127-S08}
Then the two headed off together, Shah leading so that, Varma explained, any obstacles would meet him first. {127-J08}

second.label: Heart or cosmos
second.head: Quasar beats the heart
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s genie test splits the hosts between people and physics
body: Amit Varma was explaining why the mysteries of human nature move him more than science when Ajay Shah burst out laughing. Shah had a question: if a genie offered a window into the human heart or one into a quasar fifty million light years away, which would Varma pick? {#quasar}

Varma chose the human heart, even though, he said, the quasar sometimes seems easier to grok. Shah did not hesitate. Give him two neutron stars about to crash, a camera on the scene and an observatory full of instruments, and he would take it any day. {127-S02}
Varma addressed the listeners: “Ladies, this is Ajay Shah. This is why he doesn’t ask you questions and listen well. He’s thinking of quasars.” {#ladies}

quote.text: Let me build a whole observatory with instruments there. I take it any day.

second.caption: a quasar or the human heart

third.head: Failure, the lucky break
body: Amit Varma counts his years of failure as his good fortune. Responding to Ajay Shah’s lesson that the world is complex, he said humility was the quality he was gladdest to have found, if a little late in life.

“I think when I was an arrogant young man who knew nothing, the worst thing that could have happened to me is had I succeeded,” he said. Success, a matter of luck, would have made him think himself great, and he would have stopped learning. {127-S01}
People sometimes hear his line “I failed all my life” as Bengali self-pity, he said. He calls it a blessing. {#blessing}
Those years, he said, taught him humility, “the only path to growth”, and to appreciate the complexity of other human beings, making him more empathetic.
third.caption: failing all his life

p2.title: Ten frameworks
p2.deck: Five each from Amit Varma and Ajay Shah: the ideas that shaped how they see the world

sections.label: Framework 1
sections.head: The awe of understanding
sections.caption: natural selection
body: Amit Varma’s first framework was natural selection, and he argued that it is not a subject that should only be taught in biology classes.

He discovered it through popular science writing: Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate*, then Richard Dawkins’s *The Selfish Gene* and *The Blind Watchmaker*, and Daniel Dennett’s *Consciousness Explained*. {127-R01}
His reason for caring went back to the Temple of Apollo at Delphi and its injunction, “Know thyself.” To make the most of ourselves, he said, we must understand ourselves.
Varma said he is far more drawn than Ajay Shah to fiction and the arts. The greatest mysteries for him are those of human nature: why we love, why we cry, why we feel lonely.
Natural selection, he said, helps us come to terms with these puzzles. Once you understand how you are wired, you can decide what to mitigate and what to amplify. {127-C02}
## Firmer in his atheism
Varma was an atheist long before he met the theory, and the hosts have an episode arguing that atheism is less a system of belief than a non-belief. Natural selection, he said, solidified it.
He read out Douglas Adams, who wrote that the awe natural selection inspired in him made religious awe seem silly: “I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.” {127-J10}
~ Two episodes on evolution had preceded this one, he noted, and another, on evolution in a larger context, was to come.

quote.text: Once you understand the ways in which you’re wired, you can figure out what you want to mitigate and what you want to amplify.

sections.label: Framework 2
sections.head: Nobody has the whole jigsaw
sections.caption: why the world is complex
body: If Ajay Shah could say one thing to himself at 20, it would be that the world is complex. It has taken him all the years since to understand it. {#age20}

He gave three reasons. The first is randomness. Our tidy stories about the past see only the lottery’s outcome. The Battle of Stalingrad was no done deal, he said, so any analogy to it is suspect. {#stalingrad}
The second is nonlinearity: small changes can generate large changes deep in the future.

The third is that information is spread everywhere. Each cube of air obeys the Navier-Stokes equations, but good weather forecasts would need a ridiculous amount of data. Together, he said, these should make us take three steps back. {127-C03}
## The humble firm
Inside a firm, that means humility: management should not imagine it knows everything, when tens of thousands of employees each hold little bits of information.

The opposite is arrogance. If you are so fatuous as to believe that you know, he said, “go build a China model and see how badly that works out”, pointing to Dan Wang’s recent book on the engineer’s view of the world. {127-J12}
~ The information nobody has lies in every single human being, Shah said, so good societies and organisations are those that get people to come forth with it. {#everyhuman}

quote.text: The world is more difficult to comprehend and control than we think.

sections.label: Framework 3
sections.head: No committee for language
sections.caption: spontaneous order
body: We are hardwired to treat every problem as an engineering problem, Amit Varma said: if a country isn’t running well, find the leader who will fix it. That instinct served hunter-gatherer tribes, but it is “profoundly against the reality of the world”.
The episode’s third framework was spontaneous order: things that are, in Adam Ferguson’s phrase, “the result of human action, but not human design”. {127-J13}
Matt Ridley’s *The Evolution of Everything* finds it in natural selection, language, the economy, cultural norms and common law.

No central committee decides how a language evolves. Travel through India, Varma said, and every few miles the dialect changes, each recognisable to the next village, until it has become something else entirely. {#village}
## Prices that talk

The most spectacular case, for him, is the economy, as described in Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*. Prices tell others what we want and what we lack, so that strangers a thousand miles apart can meet each other’s needs. {127-R08}
“This is sounding so sensuous already,” he admitted. {127-J05}
~ Asked by a commenter to explain spontaneous order, Varma suggested reading Ridley, then asking GPT 5 for examples and digging deep into each. {#gpt}

quote.text: People don’t realise that actually prices are a language. Prices are how we speak to each other.

sections.label: Frameworks 4 and 6
sections.head: The only gunda on the block
sections.caption: the state and the rule of law
body: Most of us are brought up to see the state as a benevolent mother, or a bit of an NGO, Ajay Shah said. Over the years he came to see this as “a wrong way of thinking”.

Max Weber supplied the first correction: the state is a community that achieves and maintains a monopoly of physical violence over a given territory. It is, in Shah’s words, “the only gunda on the block”. {127-J15}

Public choice theory supplied the second. The people who staff the state pursue their own goals, and those are not the welfare of the people. Amit Varma added his thesis that every state, with time, turns predatory. {#buchanan}
Had Shah, after years in “the belly of the beast”, always seen it this way? “It took me all my life to get these things deeply,” he replied. {127-S07}
## Written in black and white

His defence against tyranny was rule of law: an elected legislature writes compact, knowable laws, the executive only investigates, and only an independent judge can sentence. Fifty-thousand-word laws and selective enforcement, he warned, let the government find something on whoever it goes after. {#fiftyk}
~ Varma, citing Francis Fukuyama, wants an Indian state that does a few things well, beginning with rule of law. {127-C08}

quote.text: Rule of law is our only hope, is our only defence against the inevitable progression of coercive power into tyranny.

sections.label: Framework 5
sections.head: Two thank-yous, one coffee
sections.caption: the double thank-you moment
body: Ask for a coffee at a cafe, Amit Varma said, and you say thank you when the cup is handed over, and the person behind the counter says thank you when you pay. {#coffee}

This is the double thank-you moment, from an article John Stossel wrote fifteen or twenty years ago. Varma, who writes about markets all the time, said he has never managed one piece that explains their magic so fundamentally. {#stossel}

Each side values what it receives more than what it gives up, so both are better off. Our instincts, formed when an extra leg of lamb for one hunter meant less for another, are zero sum. Voluntary exchange is positive sum. {127-C06}
## Profit as philanthropy

The Angus Maddison graph of human welfare is flat until the 18th or 19th century, then explodes upwards. Technology explains part of it, Varma said, but much of it is the spread of markets, with more and more people to trade with. {#maddison}
He once wrote a column arguing that profit is the greatest philanthropy: there is no better way to make someone better off than by profiting from a voluntary exchange.
~ He has argued with Rohini Nilekani against the trichotomy of state, society and markets. Markets, he said, are a mechanism through which people in society fulfil each other’s needs. {127-J19}

quote.text: The way to maximise human welfare is to maximise double thank you moments.

sections.label: Framework 10
sections.head: Generosity without a ledger
sections.caption: giving unconditionally
body: Too many people, Ajay Shah said, are doing a hustle: trading favours, keeping IOUs and extracting better terms from the world as they climb a ladder. He gets it, he said; there is a part of that in every life.
His last framework was the alternative: “Why bother? Why keep track? Why keep accounts? Why keep score? Just give unconditionally.” {#scorekeeping}

Monitoring who owes what, he said, reflects fear, insecurity and a scarcity mindset. Giving reflects abundance, and it is in our self-interest: it makes us happier and saves the mental bandwidth spent on keeping score. {127-C13}
Freed from the ledger, you get to think about truth and beauty, he said, and some people will come back to you with “senseless acts of kindness and irrational acts of beauty”.
## A friend’s testimony
Amit Varma, who has known Shah for many years, said he has been a beneficiary of that giving himself. {127-S08}
He then made what he called a vociferous demand: generosity must extend to recommendations. {127-J07}

~ Shah obliged with Dario Amodei’s essay *Machines of Loving Grace*, on what happens as AI progresses. He is no booster of technological paradises, he said, but finds it sensible and thoughtful. {127-R18}

quote.text: And ultimately life is not about prospering, it is about flourishing.

side.boxText: Amit Varma: natural selection, spontaneous order, the double thank-you moment, playing to play, and how we spend our days. Ajay Shah: complexity, distrust of the state, rule of law, doing over watching, and giving unconditionally. Together, a toolkit for first principles thinking. {127-C01}

contQuote.text: Happiness is you are in this moment. You are with this friend, you share an interesting thought. He cracks a joke. You don’t get the joke. You laugh anyway. That is a moment.

p3.title: Tales from the toolkit
p3.deck: A grandmaster’s riddle, a borrowed want, a happy reinvention and a free day

stories.start: So here's a story. De Grand Petrosian, the famous uh Russian grandmaster,
stories.end: Then why are you playing? And Petrocian said, I'm playing to play.
stories.caption: Tigran Petrosian’s reply
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s life philosophy, borrowed from a chessboard
stories.head: Not to win, not to draw
body: In the last round of a chess tournament, the Soviet grandmaster Tigran Petrosian faced an opponent who wanted a draw. Petrosian grew deaf over time, Amit Varma noted, though that played no part in this conversation.
Hoping Petrosian wanted a draw too, the opponent leaned forward at one point and whispered: “Are you playing to win?” Petrosian shook his head.
Our man was hopeful. A couple of moves later he leaned forward again. “Are you playing to draw then?” Again Petrosian said no.
Now the opponent was confused. If Petrosian was playing neither to win nor to draw, why was he playing at all? So he asked. “I’m playing to play,” Petrosian replied. {127-S03}

Varma loved the story. He wrote a newsletter post about it. {127-R14} It has become the philosophy of his life, and his advice to every young person he speaks to: don’t play to win, don’t think of outcomes or grand goals, play for the beauty of it.
One listener had “I play to play” tattooed on his arm. Varma was “obviously very moved”, he said, though, being a little old-fashioned, he also wondered why anyone would mutilate the body. {#tattoo}

~ He reads the myth of Sisyphus the same way. Rolling a rock up a hill forever is futile only if the point is to get it to the top, he said. If the point is the rolling itself, that is your dharma, and you can be happy. {127-C09}
stories.why: Play for a win and the work becomes a means to an end, and any win soon becomes the new baseline. Play for its own sake and the joy is in the doing. {#joy}
stories.postscript: Sisyphus came up, Varma said, in his conversation with Gurcharan Das on *The Seen and the Unseen*.

stories.start: Luke Burgess wrote a book called Wanting, where he looked at the work
stories.end: It's not intrinsic. And he called this mimetic desire.
stories.caption: René Girard’s reading list
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on where our wants come from
stories.head: Wanting what they want
body: As a young man, the philosopher René Girard was asked to teach a literature course. He needed the extra pocket money, so he agreed, and compiled a reading list of the classics. {127-S04}
Then he realised something. In all of those classics, Amit Varma said, “all the heroes and heroines they want something because somebody else wants that thing.” Girard called it mimetic desire.

Luke Burgis’s *Wanting* later built on the idea to separate thick desires from thin ones. Thin desires are borrowed in search of validation: a young man wanting a Mercedes, or to be vice president. {#mercedes}

~ Thick desires are intrinsic, and can be so deep that you are not aware of them. Writing to win the Booker Prize is a thin desire, Varma said; writing for the magic of filling a blank page is a thick one. {127-C10}
stories.why: Girard’s idea came out of a side job taken for pocket money. Its lesson is personal: many of our wants are borrowed, and it takes a long time, Varma said, to get to the ones that are truly ours. {#thick}

stories.start: I I have a story about this from my life in research
stories.end: or too bad somebody's already seen them before. You also play to play.
stories.caption: reinventing what others found
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the pleasures of the research life
stories.head: Reinventing the wheel, happily
body: Ajay Shah has a story from his life in research, one he has started to see happen to many other people. His excitement is in doing research; reading papers is only a means to that end.

Very often, he said, he ends up reinventing from scratch something that others have already done. And that is okay. If the purpose is the joy of doing, you are happy; if it is a publication or a patent, you are unhappy. {127-S05}
He still reads other people, because it jogs the mind. But the primal pleasure, he said, lies in coming up with ideas and inventing things.
~ It fits his slogan that life is not a spectator sport. Doing things yourself, he said, is a hundred times more exciting than watching others do them. {#hundredx}

quote.text: You turn the key and the door opens and you see things that have never been seen before

stories.start: And I haven't had a full time job for the last seventeen, eighteen years
stories.end: doing maturgashti is how we spend our lives in happiness.
stories.caption: being master of his own time
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on living Annie Dillard’s line
stories.head: Master of his own time
body: Amit Varma has not had a full-time job for seventeen or eighteen years. The reason, he said, is that he wants to be the master of his own time. {127-S06}
As a young man he aspired to greatness: to write great books, make great movies, think great thoughts. The danger, he said, is that every day becomes a waiting room for a glorious future. {127-C12}

Now he wants to wake up looking forward to the day. He was happy, he said, with how he spent the day of the recording: shooting with Ajay Shah, chatting, doing matargashti, “one of the great terms of our times”. {127-J25}
~ Happiness, he said, is not a memory of a time you think you must have been happy. It is being in the moment with a friend who cracks a joke you don’t get, and laughing anyway. {#happiness}
stories.why: If life is an accumulation of days, a good day matters more than an impressive career. Ajay Shah’s addition: a lifetime is too big to plan, but a day is a problem you can act on. {#agency}

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah mean for years when he said he had written a “BS article”?
quiz.a: A column for the *Business Standard*, where he has written for thirty years.

quiz.q: Offered a window into the human heart or a distant quasar, which did each host choose?
quiz.a: Amit Varma chose the human heart; Ajay Shah chose the quasar without hesitating.

quiz.q: Whose definition of the state as a monopoly of physical violence did Ajay Shah use?
quiz.a: Max Weber’s, which led Shah to call the state the only gunda on the block.

quiz.q: When you buy a coffee, why do both you and the seller say thank you?
quiz.a: Each values what they receive more than what they give: a double thank-you moment.

quiz.q: What did Tigran Petrosian say when asked why he was playing, if not to win or draw?
quiz.a: “I’m playing to play,” a line Amit Varma made his life philosophy.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, what is life about, if not prospering?
quiz.a: Flourishing, he said, while making the case for giving unconditionally.
